description: Computer Engineering student interested in AI, software development, and using data to explore environmental problems. Looking for teammates interested in data analysis, mapping, or design who enjoy building practical tools.
summary:
EmberTrace is an interactive web application that explores NASA FIRMS hotspot detections across a study region encompassing Punjab and Haryana in India during September–November from 2023–2025. It combines seasonal calendars, hotspot maps, sensor comparisons, and downloadable analytics to make historical burning patterns easier to investigate.

The project addresses the MODIS–VIIRS harmonization challenge through an experimental calibration trained on 2023–2024 and evaluated on 2025. The adjustment reduces average weekly disagreement with MODIS by approximately 67% compared with unadjusted VIIRS counts. MODIS serves as a reference sensor, not ground truth. Diagnostics also reveal changing satellite acquisition times, demonstrating why simple count scaling cannot fully harmonize the records.

Motivated by air pollution concerns in northern India, the tool could help agricultural outreach teams and land managers time prevention efforts around recurring burning periods. Hotspot detections alone do not establish agricultural burning or its contribution to air pollution.
details:
EmberTrace is a web application that helps people explore burning activity in a region covering Punjab and Haryana. It uses NASA FIRMS hotspot records from MODIS and VIIRS for September through November in 2023, 2024, and 2025. Users can compare seasons through a calendar, view detections on a map, filter the records, and download data for further analysis.

The two sensors observe fires differently. VIIRS has smaller detection pixels and can record hotspots that MODIS misses. They also observe the region at different times. This means their detection counts cannot simply be combined into one consistent record.

EmberTrace takes an initial step toward making those records comparable. We use weekly counts from 2023 and 2024 to calculate an adjustment that brings VIIRS counts onto a MODIS reference scale. We then test that adjustment on 2025 without using that year to develop it. The adjustment reduces average weekly disagreement with MODIS by about 67 percent compared with unadjusted VIIRS counts. A simpler ratio method performs similarly, so we present this as an experimental starting point. MODIS is a reference sensor rather than a measure of the true number of fires.

The project was motivated by air pollution concerns in northern India. Understanding when burning repeatedly peaks could help agricultural outreach teams and land managers plan conversations, equipment access, and other support before those periods. The app supports historical exploration rather than predicting fires or measuring air quality.

We built EmberTrace using Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, and Plotly. NASA FIRMS CSV files provide the observations.

Our approach combines a visual calendar with a transparent comparison of the sensors. Users can explore patterns while also seeing the limits of the adjustment. We considered confidence flags, satellite identity, daytime and nighttime observations, and changing acquisition times. We also kept the evaluation year separate from the training years.

Hotspots are detections rather than separate fires. They do not prove agricultural burning, and missing records do not confirm that an area was observed without fire. Making these limits visible is an important part of EmberTrace.
